text.p: Stanley Gold isn't the only shareholder who has been disappointed by Koor Industries Ltd's stock market performance.

Dogged by concerns about near-term profitability and shunned by foreign institutions, Koor shares have lagged the Israeli market badly and unless there are big changes at Koor, like the kind Gold is proposing, the share's upside is limited, analysts said.
"Stanley Gold is frustrated, and correctly," said one analyst who covers Koor but declined to be identified. "We've enjoyed a rally of over 80 percent in the last year and Koor hasn't moved at all."

Koor's Tel Aviv Stock Exchange-traded shares have risen about 19 percent this year to 343.22 shekels but are off their February high of 363.54 shekels. In the meantime, the exchange's Mishtanim index of leading shares has risen nearly 45 percent.

Gold, Koor's chairman and president of its second-largest shareholder, Shamrock Holdings Ltd, said last week he wants Koor to spin off its main publicly traded holdings to shareholders in an effort to improve their returns.
The spin-offs would include Tadiran Ltd, Makhteshim Chemicals Works Ltd and Agan Chemical Manufacturers.
The proposal, however, depends on the consent of Koor's biggest shareholder, Israel's Bank Hapoalim. Since the bank itself is undergoing a change of control, no decision is imminent.

Analysts attribute part of the the sluggishness of Koor shares to the reluctance of foreign institutional investors to hold the stock. "Conglomerates underperform the overall market. Investors are more excited by pure plays," said an analyst for a foreign brokerage.

In addition, Koor's earnings are coming under pressure due to declining profitability in Koor's key telecommunications businesses, Tadiran and closely held Telrad Electronic Telecommunications Industries Ltd. Bezeq Israel Telecom, their single biggest customer, has forced them to cut prices sharply on the switching equipment it buys from them.
Earnings at Koor's closely held Nesher Cement unit are also expected to fall.
As a result, Bank Hapoalim analyst Dany Koninsky estimates that earnings per share at Koor will decline to 0.73 shekel this year and 0.70 shekel in 1998 from 0.92 shekel in 1996.
Other analysts blame Koor's president and chief executive officer, Benjamin Gaon, for failing to meet promises to make acquisitions and expand the company.

Gaon has travelled widely in search of business opportunities and at various times has made offers to buy privatisations like Israel Chemicals and El Al Israel Airlines, but he has not made a single major acquisition.
"They perceive that he has a lack of focus on the business," said one analyst. "He's disappointed investors. He's made big promises but he's not delivered anything."

Indeed, one analyst said, investors were turned off by the prospect of Koor's becoming a multinational. "People say that if Koor makes big acquisitions overseas, that dilutes it as an Israel play," he said.

Koor has a five-year strategic plan to expand its key businesses of telecommunications/electronics, agro-chemicals and building materials. However, a $200 million Yankee bond offering to help finance the programme was cancelled in June.
Most analysts say Koor is trading at about a 25 percent discount to its underlying assets after subtracting for debt, which is not excessive and could be narrowed.
"The stock has suffered from negative sentiment in the market for a long time, but the discount will inevitably narrow," said Giora Zareceanisky, an analyst at Ilanot Betchucha in Tel Aviv.
He said even given lower earnings this year, Koor's 1997 prospective price-to-earnings ratio of about 8.9 was unjustifiably low.
